title.text: Lines, yield lines, stop lines, crosswalks

why_how.text: Pavement markings steer and regulate traffic like signs do, appearing alone or beside signs and signals.
White lines divide lanes flowing the same way, while yellow lines divide opposing traffic.
White paint separates traffic flowing together, while yellow paint separates traffic flowing against each other.
Where a solid yellow line runs beside a dashed one, the solid side may not pass while the dashed side may pass when safe.
Beside a solid yellow line you must hold your lane, while beside its dashed twin you may pass when safe.

Yield lines use white, solid triangular markings aimed at approaching traffic. They identify the yielding point for three signs: Yield Here to Pedestrians and Bicycles, Yield, and Yield Here To Pedestrians.
When a sign or signal demands a stop, halt ahead of the stop line or the crosswalk, and give way to anyone inside or stepping into the crossing.
The stop line fixes where your vehicle must halt, while the crosswalk fixes where pedestrians cross and must be yielded to.
Not every crosswalk is painted, so stay alert for pedestrians at intersections with no marked crossing.
Painted crosswalks define the crossing zone, yet unpainted crossings carry the same pedestrian alert duty.

title.text: Lane arrows, reversible and shared lanes

why_how.text: Painted lane arrows dictate which moves a lane allows or requires.
Reversible lanes flip direction by time of day, usually between double-dashed yellow lines, so confirm the lane is yours from roadside signs, overhead signs, or special lights before entering.
Over a reversible lane, a green arrow opens the lane below it, a red X closes it, a flashing yellow X limits it to turns, and a steady yellow X orders you out as soon as safety allows.
Green opens the reversible lane and red closes it, while flashing yellow narrows it to turns and steady yellow evicts you.
The shared left-turn lane serves left turns from both directions with alternating arrow markings between solid-and-dashed yellow borders; you may enter and wait there but never use it to pass.

Reserved lanes belong to special vehicles by posted signs, often with a white diamond at the roadside or on the pavement; stay out unless you drive a qualifying vehicle, and the handbook's example reserves one for high-occupancy vehicles with two or more aboard.
The shared left-turn lane welcomes left turns from both directions with waiting allowed, while a reserved lane admits only its posted vehicle class.

title.text: Bike lanes, sharrows and bike boxes

why_how.text: Bike lanes are roadway slices for cyclists marked by solid white lines with bike symbols and signs, sometimes further split off by double white lines, curbs, posts, or planters.
Where a bike lane runs green, scan for cyclists before crossing the paint and never stop on it.
Drivers may cross a bike lane only to turn, first checking alongside and behind with care.
Sharrows warn drivers that bikes share the lane, promote safe passing, and curb wrong-way riding and door crashes, yet unlike bike lanes they reserve no exclusive space.
Bike lanes grant cyclists exclusive marked space, while sharrows merely announce sharing with no exclusive zone.
Bike boxes are solid-green full-lane-width zones with a cyclist image beside the crosswalk at signalized intersections, giving riders a safe turning pocket.
A pavement detector mark shows cyclists the sweet spot for tripping the traffic signal.
Green lane paint warns drivers crossing it, while the green bike box gives cyclists a full-width turning pocket at signals.
Motorists may enter bike lanes only to turn with careful checks, while cyclists use detector marks to place themselves for a signal trigger.
